I am 70 years old. I have farmed this land in Quzhou County for 50 years. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher. My household has four mouths to feed, and our 12 mu of good soil is all we have. We are lucky to have a well, so when the sky forgets to rain, we can still water our crops — though I watch the diesel cost carefully.

It is early October now, the time to sow winter wheat. I will rotary till all 12 mu to break up the maize stubble and make a fine seedbed. I buy improved wheat seed from the county supply station — it is reliable, and the straw is good for the donkey too. I will spread compound fertilizer as a base and then top-dress with urea in spring when the wheat turns green. I will irrigate three times: the overwintering water before the deep cold sets in, the jointing water when the stems shoot up, and the heading water when the grain is filling. Two sprays are enough for wheat: one herbicide and one more if the aphids or rust show up. If the weather holds fair, I expect about 1000 kg per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, there is no time to waste — the summer heat presses down hard. I will sow hybrid maize seed directly into the wheat stubble without tilling. We switched to no-tillage for maize years ago; it saves fuel, time, and my old back, and the neighbors have proven it works. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress with urea when the plants reach knee-height. I will irrigate twice: once right after sowing if the soil is dry, and again at the big flare stage when the tassels appear. For maize, I spray herbicide once and watch for corn borers — one insecticide spray is usually enough. With our well and good hybrid seed, I hope for 1100 kg per mu.

At my age, my bones ache in the morning, but my eyes are still sharp. I direct the work, and the younger members of my household run the machines. I do not try fancy new tricks — I stick with what has put food on the table for 50 years.
